new_misconceptions.message: When you multiply an equation by a number, every term must be multiplied — including the right-hand side; scale both sides equally, then subtract as normal.
When you subtract a negative number, the result gets bigger — 20 − (−2) = 22, not 18; keep track of the sign on each constant as you eliminate.
22 ÷ 11 = 2, not 3 — it’s worth pausing to check division by multiplying back: 11 × 3 = 33, which isn’t 22, so y = 2 is the correct value.
When rearranging 2x + 6 = 4, you subtract 6 from both sides to get 2x = −2, not 2x = 10 — moving a positive term to the other side changes its sign.

rationale: Minimal repair: change the RHS of the second equation from −3 to −1. The stored solutions x=−1, y=2 already satisfy eq1 (2(−1)+3(2)=4). Substituting into eq2 gives 5(−1)+2(2)=−1, so changing the constant from −3 to −1 makes both equations hold. Verification by elimination: multiply eq1 by 5 (10x+15y=20) and eq2 by 2 (10x+4y=−2), subtract to get 11y=22, y=2; back-substitute to get x=−1. Clean integer solution confirmed. One character changed (−3 → −1).
